data.source_title: Impact of Implementation of Electronically Transmitted Referrals on Pediatric Subspecialty Visit Attendance
data.locator: Abstract; Results, Visit Attendance; Table 1. Primary endpoint: referral followed by subspecialty visit within 4 weeks.
data.source_setting: Pediatric subspecialty referrals from 15 pilot general-pediatrics practices and 24 control practices in an academic children's hospital system.
data.source_period: April 2015-September 2016; pilot implementation began in 2015, with controls later receiving intervention.
data.source_n: 33,485 referral orders across all practices; pilot and control pre/post endpoint denominators vary by weekly practice-level analysis.
data.quantity: Referrals followed by attended subspecialty visit within 4 weeks, pilot practices before vs after electronic referral implementation
data.source_evidence_basis: Administrative referral and visit records showed the 4-week attendance share rose from 10.9% before to 20.0% after pilot implementation. A difference-in-differences comparison estimated an 8.6 percentage-point improvement relative to control practices.
data.limitations: Pediatric academic system and bundled quality-improvement intervention; not randomized. Difference-in-differences supports an intervention-associated change but cannot isolate each workflow component or guarantee transportability. Referral attendance is not a clinic no-show rate.
data.inferred_scenario_use: External input for modeling referral-to-scheduled-to-attended states and time-window endpoints. Keep 4-week access distinct from eventual completion; do not use these percentages as local RWJ rates.

data.source_title: Impact of Implementation of Electronically Transmitted Referrals on Pediatric Subspecialty Visit Attendance
data.locator: Results, Visit Attendance; Table 1. Secondary endpoint: referral followed by attended visit within 12 weeks.
data.source_setting: Same pediatric subspecialty referral system and pilot practices as the 4-week endpoint.
data.source_n: 33,485 referral orders across all practices; endpoint denominators vary by weekly practice-level analysis.
data.quantity: Referrals followed by attended subspecialty visit within 12 weeks, pilot practices before vs after implementation
data.source_evidence_basis: Study administrative records reported 12-week attendance increasing from 19.6% before electronic referral implementation to 34.2% after implementation.
data.limitations: Pediatric academic setting; nonrandomized QI evaluation. The before/after association does not prove causality, and 12-week completion is sensitive to appointment availability, family access, and clinically appropriate deferral.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Represent longer referral follow-up windows separately from near-term access. Do not infer an appointment wait-time distribution or apply the observed change locally.

data.source_title: Impact of Implementation of Electronically Transmitted Referrals on Pediatric Subspecialty Visit Attendance
data.locator: Results, Processes of Care; percentage of referrals with appointments scheduled within 4 and 12 weeks.
data.source_setting: Same pediatric subspecialty referral system and pilot practices.
data.source_n: 33,485 referral orders across all practices; process denominators vary by week and practice.
data.quantity: Referrals with appointment scheduled within 4 and 12 weeks, pilot practices before vs after
data.source_evidence_basis: The authors report that referral scheduling within both four and twelve weeks improved after the electronically transmitted referral process was introduced.
data.limitations: Nonrandomized process redesign at a pediatric academic institution. Aggregate window endpoints do not reveal the distribution of actual lead times or distinguish clinic capacity from family contact and decision delays.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use as a reference for referral-processing and appointment-scheduled milestones; model referral receipt, family contact, slot availability, and attendance as distinct transitions requiring local calibration.

data.source_title: Impact of Implementation of Electronically Transmitted Referrals on Pediatric Subspecialty Visit Attendance
data.locator: Results, Balancing Measures; nonattendance among referrals scheduled within 4 weeks.
data.source_setting: Same pediatric subspecialty referral system; pilot practices.
data.source_n: Denominator is scheduled referrals with visit dates within 4 weeks; exact group counts not provided in the reported passage.
data.quantity: Nonattendance among scheduled referrals within 4 weeks, before vs after intervention
data.source_evidence_basis: The study tracked nonattendance as a balancing measure and found no statistically significant increase after scheduling improved.
data.limitations: The result is conditional on an appointment being scheduled and is not a no-show rate for all referrals. Nonattendance definition and pediatric population may differ from other systems; nonsignificance is not proof of equivalence.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Keep appointment scheduling and subsequent cancellation/no-show as separate model transitions. Use this only as an external balancing-measure example, not an RWJ attendance parameter.
